one_line_takeaway: Fine-tuning a non-instruction-tuned base model for one fixed task removes the instruction-following that prompt injection exploits, cutting attack success from ~87% to ~0.5% with under 2% quality loss.
core_contribution: The paper introduces Jatmo, a framework for building task-specific LLMs that are robust to prompt-injection attacks by construction. Its key insight is that only instruction-tuned models can be hijacked by injected instructions, so Jatmo instead fine-tunes a NON-instruction-tuned base model (OpenAI's davinci-002) to perform a single fixed task. A trusted instruction-tuned "teacher" model (GPT-3.5-Turbo) is used only on benign inputs to generate output labels R_i = M(P + D_i) for a dataset of task inputs {D_i}; the base model is then fine-tuned on the {D_i, R_i} pairs so that at deployment the app calls F(D) instead of M(P + D). Because the fine-tuned model was never trained to seek and follow instructions in its input, it ignores malicious instructions embedded in data. The design is explicitly inspired by SQL query parameterization (cited prior art, not their invention): it separates trusted control (the fixed prompt P, baked into the model) from untrusted data D. A secondary contribution is a fully automated synthetic-data pipeline (seed generation, input generation, input formatting via GPT-4) so Jatmo can be applied even with a single example or zero examples of task inputs, making it a drop-in replacement for a normal LLM call. The authors claim this is the first effective defense against prompt injection.
threat_model: Attacker fully controls the input data D fed to an LLM-integrated application but has no control over the legitimate/developer-written instruction P; no query or weight access to the victim model is assumed, and the attacker need not know P. The attack succeeds only if the victim model executes the injected malicious instruction instead of the legitimate task (goal hijacking); merely causing the model to fail the legitimate task is treated as denial-of-service and does not count. The focus is indirect prompt injection against API/application settings (e.g., RAG, web-browsing agents, email/customer-service bots); defending web-chat direct-injection/jailbreak is explicitly out of scope. Jatmo also defends prompt-leaking but the evaluation centers on goal hijacking.
limitations: One task-specific model must be trained per unique prompt P, with an up-front fine-tuning cost, making Jatmo unsuitable for interactive chat where each prompt is used once; it sacrifices general-purpose versatility. It defends only prompt injection, not jailbreaks against alignment or adversarial examples. It fundamentally depends on being able to fine-tune non-instruction-tuned base models, which providers are increasingly not offering (fine-tuning an already instruction-tuned model would not confer robustness). The security evaluation covers only currently-known injection strategies (HackAPrompt level-1 generics plus manually crafted attacks) and the authors acknowledge stronger unseen attacks may exist; the exact-match "HACKED" success metric can under-count partial compromises. Labels for both fine-tuning and rating come from GPT-3.5-Turbo, so quality is measured relative to the teacher rather than absolute ground truth.
